prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I ranked optical lattice clocks only eighth in my opening ballot, and I now think that was too low. I weighted the cosmology and astroparticle entries by how directly they speak to the dark sector, which is a personal bias of mine. Reading the colleagues' ballots, the case for B004 is the strongest and the most independently argued on the table. Four members rank it first, a fifth ranks it third, and their reasons are not the same. The measurement idea is original (the magic-wavelength lattice that cancels light shifts) and it was realised. Fractional uncertainties near 1e-18 have been reproduced in many national laboratories and across continents. It also bears on questions I care about, because it tests the constancy of constants and measures gravitational redshift over millimetre distances, so nature is being asked a sharp question with a new instrument. The credit is unusually clean: Katori for the concept and the first strontium lattice clock, Ye for taking the performance to the frontier. That is exactly the situation in which, as Secretary, I find that the choice 'feels obvious' once the work is done.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is overlap with earlier prizes: the 2005 frequency-comb award to Hall and Hansch was a precondition, and Wineland's 2012 prize covered ion control and ion clocks. A committee could read the lattice clock as a continuation of metrology already honoured. The redefinition of the second has also not happened, so part of the practical payoff is still promised rather than delivered. Finally, B004 is an instrument and metrology achievement rather than a new phenomenon, and I would not want the committee to treat 'seven of eight members have it on the ballot' as a substitute for scientific argument.

responses.point: Lindroth places B004 first as precision-meets-theory atomic physics, with a clean two-person credit and a mature, internationally confirmed result, while noting that Hall and Hansch (2005) might make clocks look like a continuation.
responses.response: I agree with the merit argument and I think her own caveat is answered by the physics. The comb made it possible to count optical cycles. It did not contain the idea of trapping neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so that thousands of atoms can be interrogated without Doppler or recoil shifts. That is a separate invention and it produced a separate step in accuracy. I would, however, want the citation to name the lattice concept explicitly so the distinction from 2005 and 2012 is visible in the text. Where I stay slightly cautious is her phrase about the clocks testing 'stability of constants'. Those tests are real but so far give null results, so I would justify the prize by the capability and not by a fundamental discovery.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, because the Bistritzer-MacDonald magic-angle prediction preceded the 2018 experiments, a theory-to-experiment link he values most, and he places clocks only sixth, deferring to AMO colleagues.
responses.response: I share his criterion, since a prediction that nature then confirms is the kind of theory I trust, and it is why B010 stays near the top of my own list as my first alternative. But I disagree on ordering. He himself concedes that the superconducting pairing mechanism is unresolved and that the field is only about eight years old, and it is exactly the kind of case where the long-term meaning is not yet settled. I also note that Yuan Cao, the first author of the 2018 experiments, is outside the credited set, which makes the fairness question sharper than it is for B004. I would not call this a reason to reject the candidate, only a reason to wait one more cycle while the lattice clock, which is settled, goes first.

responses.point: Pearce, the chair, ranks clocks first and IceCube second, and argues that IceCube is a new observational window whose attribution is hard because Halzen and Karle lead a collaboration of hundreds, and he doubts Yoshida's case is as strong.
responses.response: I agree with his reading of IceCube, and I ranked it second myself. His reservation that the origin of the bulk of the diffuse flux is unresolved is fair. The diffuse flux is firm, but the individual source associations (TXS 0506+056, the Galactic plane) are still at modest significance and KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are only partially independent. This is why I move it to second place and not to the top. On names, I would also keep the credit to Halzen and Karle and not extend it to Yoshida, because I could not defend a larger set on the evidence in the ballots. I would revisit IceCube in a year or two, when more independent confirmation is in hand.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first because it created a new quantum-optical regime, strong coupling of one artificial atom to one microwave photon on a chip, that underlies superconducting processors, and he flags both his proximity to the field and the overlap with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I respect his flagging of the conflict, and I think the scientific case is real. But I would put the 2025 overlap more heavily than he does. A prize on macroscopic quantum behaviour in superconducting circuits has only just been given, and the committee should not look as if it is rewarding the same family of devices twice in quick succession. The attribution between Blais and Girvin is also unresolved, as he admits, and Kroll proposes a different trio from his. Two members disagree on who the three are, which suggests the credit is less settled than for B004. I am not against circuit QED in principle, and I would want to hear the argument again in a later round.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see optical lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize, and whether the citation can make that distinction explicit.
Whether the formal redefinition of the SI second should come first, or whether the measured performance already justifies the award now.

Whether other early contributors to optical lattice clocks (for example Lemonde and Takamoto) are outside the credited names and could be argued to deserve a place, as several colleagues noted without being able to resolve it.
How the committee should treat Jun Ye's appearance in other candidacies when deciding on the final configuration.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred B004 configuration. My connections (David Gross as PhD supervisor, Thomas Van Riet as co-author, and the Uppsala string-theory group) are not related to any shortlisted candidate. I note for transparency that my opening top choice, the baryon acoustic oscillation entry B045, is in my own field of cosmology, and I treat that familiarity as a bias to discount, not as a reason for preference.
